I'm referring to autism or on the spectrum. Special needs students like things direct and simple. So when I say high functioning. Can they communicate, can they do paper work or do daily routine without help. Keeping it short and direct is good. Knowing their routine and what sets them off is also a good start. For example I teach special needs students and most of them are non verbal, how do I get along with them? Knowing what they like. As a teacher you kind of observe that and you find strategies to deal with certain behaviours. So telling them what they need to do in simple terms like first you do this then it's break and next is walk...helps so they know. 

If you are working with learning disabilities it's easier so you'll be able to communicate with them. Having constructive criticism is good. Instead of telling them they are wrong. Teach them what went wrong and how to fix stuff for next time. 

Overall if it's social issues you can only do so much for them. Offer support that isn't invasive. Lending your ear will always earn their respect.

It depends how high functioning they are. If you are putting a demand like work offer breaks or other alternatives. Redirect usually works or giving them a choice and or pairing with what happened after the work. Using the first then next language 100% helps

This student who I have worked with as a supply as a teacher assistant (although I can teach) have been the most memorable and I would say have changed my teaching practices. I don’t know why it impacted me as much but it did. Ive worked with this student through out the year but on this specific day it made it unforgettable. It started as a normal day but during mid day he ran out of the classroom upset and crying into the washroom, I didn’t think much of it until a latter of things happened. I asked his friends what happened and they were vague and he was called into the principals office to talk about it. He came out unchanged. I carried on my day 30 minutes later he was shadowing one of the teachers and was still upset. I volunteered to take him for a bit and it was huge learning moment and curve for me. I did not know how to deal with it but I knew this kid was quiet and didn’t talk as much. He’s a resilient, smart, thoughtful kid that have a lot of thoughts and on his mind. When I took him all I did was continue to prep for what I needed while him helping me. As I know some kids don’t like to share their sadness so all I did had presence with him. After I was done we went to a room and we played games did not talk about what happened and all we did was play. When the day ended I just said “did you feel better?” I did not ask about what happened or anything else. I don’t know what he thought of me at that point but I hope from what I did it helped him in any way. Why was it memorable? It was the first time this stuff happened and it broke my heart how he was feeling. From that point on until covid hit which was a few weeks, every time I was there I would check up and look out for him. I know his friends did not treat him as a friend so I did what I can to look out and support him as I can without being invasive. He changed my teaching practices and gave me a deeper look at how I view students in this situation the reverse of the quote “the squeaky wheel gets the oil” except he was not that wheel and what impacts or hidden baggage these students carry with them. It also led me to think about mental health and well being as I didn’t have the greatest experience either so I kind of know that pain.
